lead: You'll describe the one-page internal page you're going to build for your team in this level, and have Cowork save it in a short notes file in your folder.
why: Cowork starts each task fresh. A notes file in your folder means you explain your project once, not every time.
result: A notes file in your Cowork Academy folder that describes your team page project.

think.scene: At work: a school business manager keeps a notes file for each project, so Cowork never needs the same background twice.
think.ask: Which project, client or process would you want Cowork to remember, so you never re-explain it?

steps.goal: Tell Cowork what team page you plan to build, so it saves the background in a notes file and you never have to explain it again.
steps.title: Describe your team page project
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task, change the part in square brackets, and press Enter. Use roles or first names only, and leave out customer details, phone numbers and passwords.
steps.prompt: I'm new to Cowork. Over the next few missions I'll build a one-page internal page for my team at work. My team: [your team and what it does, e.g. the accounts payable team, we pay supplier invoices, or the HR team, we onboard new hires]. Save a short file called project-notes.md in this folder that says what the page is for, who will use it, and what it should include. Keep it under 10 lines.
steps.see: Cowork confirms it saved project-notes.md, and the file appears in your Cowork Academy folder. It's a plain file you can open and edit yourself.
steps.stuck: If Cowork asks you questions about the page first, answer them in a sentence or two. Plain English is fine, there's no wrong answer.

steps.goal: Read what Cowork wrote, because every later task will rely on this file and a mistake here would repeat everywhere.
steps.title: Check the notes are accurate
steps.do: Open project-notes.md from your Cowork Academy folder and read it. If anything is wrong, tell Cowork in the same task what to change.
steps.see: A few short lines describing your team, who the page is for and what it should include, in words you recognize. Notice whether it reads like your team, in your words.
steps.stuck: If the file opens in an app you don't expect, that's fine. Any text editor or browser can show it.

steps.goal: Prove the notes work: a brand-new task should know your project only by reading the file, not from memory.
steps.title: Test that a new task remembers
steps.do: Start another new task in your Cowork Academy folder. Paste this in and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Read project-notes.md in this folder and tell me in one sentence what my team page project is about.
steps.see: One sentence that matches your project, even though this is a brand-new task. Notice that Cowork knew this without you explaining it again.
steps.stuck: If Cowork says it can't find the file, check that the new task is using your Cowork Academy folder, not a different one.

steps.q: On Monday you start a new task and ask Cowork to add a section to your team page. What lets Cowork know the project without you explaining it again?
options: Cowork remembers last week's tasks by itself
It reads project-notes.md in the folder
You described it fully in an earlier task
steps.why: A new task can read files in its folder, so project-notes.md carries your background forward. It does not see what you typed in earlier tasks, however detailed that was.

lead: You'll have Cowork build a one-page internal page for your team, with what you do, who to contact and useful links, then improve its design with Claude's help.
why: Turning an idea into a working page in an afternoon means your team gets a useful page now, instead of waiting weeks for someone else.
result: A designed one-page team page, index.html, in your Cowork Academy folder, improved with design feedback.

think.scene: At work: an HR coordinator at a manufacturer builds a one-page onboarding site for new hires in an afternoon, instead of waiting weeks for IT.
think.ask: What page would your team or customers use tomorrow if it existed?

steps.goal: Have Cowork turn your project notes into a real web page for your team, so you see an idea become something you can open in minutes.
steps.title: Build your team page
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task, change the part in square brackets, and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Read project-notes.md in this folder (if it's missing, my team is [your team and what it does, e.g. the sales operations team, we keep quotes and pricing moving]). Build a one-page internal page for my team and save it as index.html. Include a headline, a short What we do section, a Who to contact section with roles, and a list of useful links. Use placeholder names I can edit later. Make it clean and easy to read.
steps.see: Cowork confirms it saved index.html, and the file appears in your Cowork Academy folder. This is the first draft, which you'll improve in the next steps.
steps.stuck: Don't have project-notes.md? That's fine. The part in square brackets tells Cowork enough to build the page.

steps.goal: See the draft the way your team would, because you can only judge the design once you've looked at the real page.
steps.title: Open the page in your browser
steps.do: Open index.html from your Cowork Academy folder. It opens in your web browser.
steps.see: Your team page in the browser, with a headline and sections for what you do, who to contact and useful links. Notice anything that feels cramped or plain, since that's what you'll ask Cowork to improve next.
steps.stuck: If you see code instead of a web page, the file opened in a text editor. Right-click it and choose to open it with your web browser.

steps.goal: Ask Cowork to review its own page like a designer, so you get three specific improvements instead of guessing what to fix.
steps.title: Get a design critique
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Give my page a quick design critique. List the 3 changes that would improve it most, in plain English.
steps.see: A short numbered list of design suggestions, such as more space around the headline or clearer section headings. Notice which two you'd pick for the next step.

steps.goal: Choose the two suggestions that matter most and have Cowork apply them, which finishes your improved team page.
steps.title: Apply two chosen changes
steps.do: Paste this into the same task with the 2 suggestions you like, and press Enter. Then refresh the page in your browser.
steps.prompt: Apply suggestions [the numbers you like, e.g. 1 and 3] to index.html.
steps.see: After refreshing, the page shows the changes you picked. Compare it with your first version to see the difference.
steps.stuck: If nothing looks different, refresh the browser tab again, or reopen index.html from the folder.

steps.q: Your manager says the top of your team page looks cramped. Which request to Cowork will most likely fix it in one try?
options: Add more space around the headline
Make the whole page look more professional
Rebuild the page from scratch with a new design
steps.why: A specific request tells Cowork exactly what to change. Asking for a more professional look leaves it guessing, and rebuilding throws away the parts that already work.

lead: You'll ask Cowork which skills it has, then use one of them to improve your team page.
why: Skills are ready-made abilities. Knowing they exist means you can ask for expert help with a task instead of starting from nothing.
result: Your team page improved with the help of one Cowork skill.

think.scene: At work: a marketer at a software company uses a built-in skill to turn rough meeting notes into a polished brief in seconds.
think.ask: Which writing or formatting chore do you repeat every week?

steps.goal: Find out which ready-made skills Cowork can use and which one fits your page best, so you don't need to know any skill names.
steps.title: See what skills Cowork has
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: What skills do you have available right now? List them in plain English, with one line on what each is good for. Then look at index.html in this folder and tell me which one skill would improve it most, and why.
steps.see: A list of skills with short descriptions, followed by one recommended skill and a sentence or two on how it would help your page. Notice which skill it recommends and the reason it gives.
steps.stuck: Don't have index.html? First paste: "Make a quick one-page internal page for my team and save it as index.html." Then paste the prompt above.

steps.goal: Use the recommended skill on index.html, so you see a skill do real work on a file you already have.
steps.title: Apply the skill to your page
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter. Then open index.html from your Cowork Academy folder, or refresh it, to see the change.
steps.prompt: Use that skill to improve index.html, and tell me what you changed.
steps.see: A short summary of what changed, and the updated page in your browser. Notice what it improved that you might not have thought to ask for.
steps.stuck: If Cowork shows the result only in the task and the page hasn't changed, paste: "Please update index.html with that."

steps.q: A teammate in finance says they can't use Cowork skills because they don't know any skill names. What do you tell them?
options: Skills only work if you type the exact name
Skills are only for building web pages
Ask Cowork to list its skills first
steps.why: Cowork can list the skills it has and suggest one that fits your file, so you don't need to memorize names. Skills cover many kinds of work, not only web pages.

lead: You'll have Cowork turn a messy team email thread about late deliveries into a clear customer update letter to Dr. Okafor, saved as a real Word document.
why: Cowork makes real files you can edit and send, not only answers in a task, and it can turn scattered notes into something a busy customer can read in a minute.
result: A Word document customer update letter in your Cowork Academy folder, opened and checked against the notes.

think.scene: At work: a paralegal at a law firm turns a messy email thread into a clean status update for a client.
think.ask: Which document do you rewrite from scratch every time?

steps.goal: Have Cowork turn a messy team email thread into a short customer letter, using only facts from the notes.
steps.title: Ask for the customer letter
steps.do: team-notes.txt is already in your Cowork Academy folder. Paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Read team-notes.txt in this folder. Write a short, friendly update letter to Dr. Okafor at Desert Bloom Clinics about the late deliveries: what's been happening, what we are doing about it, and what happens next. Keep it short enough to read on a phone. Use only facts from the notes. Save it as a Word document called customer-update-desert-bloom.docx.
steps.see: Cowork confirms it saved customer-update-desert-bloom.docx, and the file appears in your Cowork Academy folder. Notice it's a real Word file, not just text in the task.
steps.stuck: If Cowork can't find team-notes.txt, check that this task is using your Cowork Academy folder. If the file is missing, download the starter folder again from the setup mission.

steps.goal: Check Cowork's facts yourself, because a letter that goes to a customer must match the source notes exactly.
steps.title: Check the letter against the notes
steps.do: Open customer-update-desert-bloom.docx from your Cowork Academy folder. Compare the numbers in it with team-notes.txt.
steps.see: A formatted one-page letter to Dr. Okafor that mentions the late deliveries since July, how many of Desert Bloom's orders were late, and the carrier change, matching the notes. Notice whether each number is the same in both.
steps.stuck: If you don't have Word, the file also opens in Google Docs, Pages or another word processor.

steps.goal: Practice asking for one specific edit to the saved file, which is how you'd tailor a letter before sending it.
steps.title: Change one thing in the letter
steps.do: Close the file. Then paste this into the same task, change the part in square brackets, and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Update customer-update-desert-bloom.docx: [one change, e.g. make it shorter and put the plan in the first paragraph].
steps.see: Cowork confirms the update. When you reopen the letter, the change is there.
steps.stuck: If Cowork says it can't save the file, make sure the letter is closed in Word, then ask again.

steps.q: Dr. Okafor calls before your letter arrives and asks how many of Desert Bloom Clinics' orders have been delivered late. What do the team notes say?
options: 19 orders
26 orders
25 orders
steps.why: team-notes.txt says 26 late orders for Desert Bloom Clinics. The other numbers are real too (19 is their ticket count, 25 is West delivery tickets), so check which one the letter uses before you send it.

lead: You'll have Cowork build a support tracker in Excel from the practice support tickets, with totals that add themselves up, then see the formulas work.
why: Spreadsheets with working formulas save you from adding up numbers by hand and copying last month's file.
result: An Excel support tracker in your Cowork Academy folder, with totals that update automatically and a chart.

think.scene: At work: a finance lead at a clinic group has Cowork build a tracker with working formulas, instead of copying and patching last month's file.
think.ask: Which spreadsheet do you rebuild or update by hand?

steps.goal: Have Cowork sum up the practice support tickets by category in a spreadsheet, with a total row that calculates itself.
steps.title: Build the support tracker
steps.do: support-tickets.csv is already in your Cowork Academy folder. Paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Open support-tickets.csv in this folder. Create an Excel spreadsheet called support-tracker.xlsx with one row per ticket category, showing its number of tickets and total credit issued, sorted from highest credit to lowest. Add a total row at the bottom that uses SUM formulas, so it updates when a number changes.
steps.see: Cowork confirms it saved support-tracker.xlsx, and the file appears in your Cowork Academy folder. Notice the rows are sorted by credit issued, not by number of tickets.
steps.stuck: If Cowork can't find support-tickets.csv, use the download link below to get it, save it in your Cowork Academy folder, and paste the prompt again.

steps.goal: Prove the totals are real formulas by changing a number and watching the total move, so you can trust the file later.
steps.title: Test that the total updates
steps.do: Open support-tracker.xlsx from your Cowork Academy folder. Change one category's credit amount and press Enter. Then close the file without saving.
steps.see: The total at the bottom changes by itself to match your new number.
steps.stuck: If the total doesn't change, click on it. If you see a plain number instead of something like =SUM(...), paste into the task: "Make the totals SUM formulas."

steps.goal: Turn the table into a bar chart so you can see at a glance which category costs the most credit.
steps.title: Add a credit chart
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter. Then reopen support-tracker.xlsx.
steps.prompt: Add a bar chart to support-tracker.xlsx that shows the total credit issued for each ticket category.
steps.see: A bar chart in the spreadsheet with one bar per category, with the tallest bar for the category with the most credit. Notice which bar is tallest, since that's the answer to the check question.
steps.stuck: If Cowork says it can't save the file, make sure support-tracker.xlsx is closed in Excel, then ask again.

steps.q: Your manager asks which kind of support ticket has cost the company the most in credits since April. What does your tracker show?
options: Delivery
Product issue
Billing
steps.why: Delivery tickets top the tracker at $2,525 in credits. Product issue is second at $1,560, and Billing is third at $1,040 even though it has the most tickets, so ticket count alone would mislead you.

lead: You'll have Cowork design a few simple logo options for your team page as SVG files, pick one, and add it to the page.
why: Making a simple visual yourself means you don't have to wait on a designer for every small graphic.
result: A logo file, such as logo-2.svg, in your Cowork Academy folder, shown on your team page.

think.scene: At work: a nonprofit's communications team designs simple logos and icons for its internal pages without waiting for a designer.
think.ask: Where do you wait on someone else for a visual?

steps.goal: Have Cowork draw three simple logos for your team page, so you can compare real options instead of imagining them.
steps.title: Design three logo options
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task, change the parts in square brackets, and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Read project-notes.md in this folder (if it's missing, my team is [your team and what it does, e.g. the customer service team, we answer questions about orders]). Design 3 simple logo options for my team page in a [style, e.g. clean and modern, or warm and friendly] style. Save them in this folder as SVG files called logo-1.svg, logo-2.svg and logo-3.svg.
steps.see: Three files, logo-1.svg, logo-2.svg and logo-3.svg, appear in your Cowork Academy folder.
steps.stuck: If Cowork shows the logos only in the task, paste: "Save each logo as an SVG file in this folder."

steps.goal: Pick the logo that fits your team, or tell Cowork what to change, because you decide the look and Cowork draws it.
steps.title: Choose your favorite logo
steps.do: Open the three logo files from your Cowork Academy folder and choose one. If none feels right, tell Cowork in the same task what to change.
steps.see: You have one logo you like. Notice what you'd change in the others, which helps you give clearer feedback.
steps.stuck: If a logo opens as code, right-click it and choose to open it with your web browser. Be specific about changes, for example "simpler shapes" or "use navy instead of green".

steps.goal: Place your chosen logo on index.html, so the logo and the page come together as your finished team page.
steps.title: Put the logo on your page
steps.do: Paste this into the same task with the number of your favorite, and press Enter. Then open or refresh index.html.
steps.prompt: Add logo-[your pick, e.g. 2].svg to the top of index.html, next to the headline, at a sensible size.
steps.see: Your team page shows the logo at the top.
steps.stuck: Don't have index.html? Paste this first: "Make a quick one-page internal page for my team and save it as index.html." If the logo doesn't show, paste: "The logo isn't showing on index.html. Please fix it."

steps.q: Your team lead likes your logo but says it looks too busy at the small size in the page header. What's the best next step?
options: Use it anyway, since it's only for the team
Ask for a brand-new set of logo ideas
Ask for a simpler version of it
steps.why: Clear feedback on the logo you already like usually gets you there in one more try. Starting over loses what works, and a busy logo makes the page harder to read.

lead: You'll give Cowork a real work question and get back a short summary, with the sources it used.
why: A sourced summary in minutes replaces an hour of clicking through search results, as long as you check the sources.
result: A short, sourced research summary on a work question you chose.

think.scene: At work: a bank's relationship manager preps for a client meeting with a sourced one-page brief on the client's industry, built in five minutes.
think.ask: What do you look up by hand before meetings or decisions?

steps.goal: Give Cowork a real question from your job and get a short answer with links, so you can see where each claim comes from.
steps.title: Ask a sourced work question
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task, change the question in square brackets, and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Search the web and research this for me: [a work question, e.g. what are the most common reasons business customers switch suppliers, and how do suppliers prevent it]. Give me the key points in 5 short bullets, and list the sources you used with links.
steps.see: Five bullet points answering your question, followed by a list of web sources with links. Notice that each bullet should trace back to a listed source.
steps.stuck: If the answer is too general, make the question more specific, with an industry, region or time frame. If Cowork says it can't search the web, check Claude's help center at support.claude.com, or ask your Academy program contact.

steps.goal: Open one source and verify the fact, because Cowork can misread a page and you're the one who answers for it.
steps.title: Check one source yourself
steps.do: Click one of the source links and find the fact Cowork took from it.
steps.see: The page supports what Cowork said in its summary. If it doesn't, you've caught a mistake before it spread.
steps.stuck: If the page doesn't say what Cowork claimed, paste into the same task: "This source doesn't support that point. Please check it."

steps.goal: Ask a second question that builds on the first answer, which is how a quick search turns into useful research.
steps.title: Dig deeper with a follow-up
steps.do: Type one follow-up question into the same task, based on what you learned, and press Enter.
steps.prompt: [your follow-up, e.g. Which of these would be cheapest for a team like ours to try first, and why?]
steps.see: A focused answer that builds on the first summary. Notice that it uses what the first summary already said.

steps.q: Cowork's summary says a new data-privacy rule takes effect next month. You want to tell your team today. What do you do first?
options: Open the source and confirm the rule
Share it, since Cowork listed its sources
Share it with a note that Cowork found it
steps.why: Claude can misread a page or mix up places and dates. A listed source only helps if you open it and check that it says what the summary claims.

lead: You'll connect one company-approved app, such as your work calendar, and have Cowork read one thing from it.
why: Connectors let Cowork find information in the apps you already use, so you stop clicking through them yourself.
result: One connected, company-approved app, and real information Cowork read from it. Or a practice summary from customer-messages.txt.

think.scene: At work: an office coordinator at a law firm asks "what's on my calendar this week and what needs prep?" instead of clicking through three apps.
think.ask: Which app do you open most just to find information?

steps.goal: Find out which app your company allows you to connect, so you stay inside company rules before touching any connector.
steps.title: Pick an approved app
steps.do: Only connect apps your company has approved. Ask your manager or Academy program contact which app you can connect, such as your work calendar.
steps.see: You know one approved app to connect, or you know there isn't one yet.
steps.stuck: No approved app yet? Skip the next step and use the practice prompt in the last step's tip instead.

steps.goal: Link the app to Cowork by signing in yourself, so Cowork can read from it without ever seeing your password.
steps.title: Connect the approved app
steps.do: Connect the approved app. For directions, check Claude's help center at support.claude.com. A sign-in window opens and you sign in yourself with your work account.
steps.see: The app shows as connected in Cowork.
steps.stuck: If the sign-in window doesn't appear, check whether your browser blocked a pop-up, then try again. If you're still stuck, ask your Academy program contact.

steps.goal: Have Cowork read and summarize one thing from the app, without changing anything, to see how a connector saves you clicking through it.
steps.title: Have Cowork read one thing
steps.do: Only if your company has approved this connector. Otherwise, use customer-messages.txt. Paste this into your Cowork task, choose the example that fits your app, and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Using the app I connected, read [one thing, e.g. my calendar events for the next 7 days] and summarize it in short bullets. Don't send, change or delete anything.
steps.see: A short summary of real information from your app, such as next week's meetings. Notice that nothing was sent, changed or deleted.
steps.stuck: No approved app? Paste this instead: "Read customer-messages.txt in this folder and summarize the 8 messages in short bullets. Don't reply to anything." If Cowork can't reach your connected app, ask your Academy program contact.

steps.q: You've connected your company-approved calendar and want a summary of next week's meetings. What should your prompt include?
options: Your calendar password, so it can sign in
Not to send, change or delete anything
Permission to accept invites for you
steps.why: Telling Cowork not to send, change or delete anything keeps a reading task a reading task. You sign in yourself in a pop-up, so Cowork never needs your password.

lead: You'll tell Cowork what you did in this level, get a plain-English recap, and save it into your project notes file.
why: A saved recap shows what you can now do, and gives future tasks the full picture of your project.
result: An updated project-notes.md with a recap of your first build.

think.scene: At work: the best ideas come from naming the boring parts of the job out loud.
think.ask: Name three tasks from this week that felt like copy-and-paste work.

steps.goal: Have Cowork list your files and describe what you made in this level, so you see how much you've built.
steps.title: Get a recap of your build
steps.do: Paste this into your Cowork task, change the part in square brackets to match what you did, and press Enter.
steps.prompt: List the files in this folder. Then write a short recap of what I built in Cowork Academy, in plain English bullets. Here's what I did: [what you did, e.g. built a team page, wrote a customer update letter, made a support tracker, designed a logo, used a skill, connected my calendar].
steps.see: A list of the files in your folder, then a bulleted recap that names what you built, such as index.html, the customer letter and the tracker.
steps.stuck: If the recap misses something or adds something you didn't do, tell Cowork, for example: "I didn't connect an app. Please remove that."

steps.goal: Add the recap to project-notes.md, so future tasks start with the full picture of your project.
steps.title: Save the recap in your notes
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: Add that recap to the end of project-notes.md under a heading called What I built. Don't change the rest of the file. If project-notes.md doesn't exist, create it.
steps.see: Cowork confirms it updated or created project-notes.md.

steps.goal: Confirm the recap landed and your original notes are intact, since this file carries your work into later missions.
steps.title: Check the notes file
steps.do: Open project-notes.md from your Cowork Academy folder.
steps.see: Your original project description at the top, and the new What I built section at the end. Notice that nothing from your first description was lost.
steps.stuck: If your original notes are gone, paste into the task: "Please put back my original project description at the top."

steps.q: Next month you'll start a new task to add a section to your team page, and you want Cowork to know what you've built. What works best?
options: Expect Cowork to recall this month's tasks
Let Cowork guess from the file names
Keep the recap in project-notes.md
steps.why: A new task doesn't see earlier tasks, but it can read files in your folder. File names alone don't say what each file is for or what you decided.

lead: You'll put your team page online with GitHub Pages, a free service, so your team can open it from a link.
why: Optional: a link is easier to share than a file, but setup takes 30 minutes or more, and anyone with the link can see the page.
result: Your team page online, with a link that opens in any browser. Or a page checked and ready to share on your team's drive.

think.scene: At work: a store operations team at a retailer shares one link to a page instead of emailing attachments around.
think.ask: What would you rather share as a link than as a file?

steps.goal: Have Cowork scan your page for anything private before it goes online, because a published page is public to anyone with the link.
steps.title: Check the page for private details
steps.do: Ask your manager before you publish a team page. Then paste this into your Cowork task and press Enter.
steps.prompt: I may publish index.html online, where anyone with the link can see it. Check it for anything that shouldn't be public, like mobile numbers, personal emails, passwords or access codes, customer names, prices or internal notes, and list what you find.
steps.see: A short list of details that shouldn't be public, or a note that there are none.
steps.stuck: If something is listed, ask Cowork to remove it from index.html before you go on. If your manager would rather keep the page internal, put index.html on your team's shared drive instead and stop here. Don't have index.html? Ask Cowork to make a quick one-page team page first.

steps.goal: Have Cowork guide you one step at a time through publishing, so you can put the page online with no prior experience.
steps.title: Walk through GitHub Pages publishing
steps.do: Paste this into the same task and press Enter. Follow each step and say done after each one. You create the GitHub account and sign in yourself.
steps.prompt: Walk me through publishing index.html, and any logo file it uses, for free with GitHub Pages. I'm a complete beginner. Give me one step at a time and wait for me to say done before the next one.
steps.see: One step at a time, ending with a link that looks like yourname.github.io.
steps.stuck: If a step doesn't match your screen, describe what you see to Cowork. If your company doesn't allow GitHub, stop here and share the file on your team's drive instead.

steps.goal: Open the link as a visitor would, to confirm the page and logo load correctly from the internet.
steps.title: Open your live page
steps.do: Open your link in a new browser tab.
steps.see: Your team page, with its headline and logo, loading from the internet.
steps.stuck: A new site can take a few minutes to appear. If the link shows an error, wait 5 minutes and try again. If the logo is missing, tell Cowork. The file may not have been uploaded.

steps.q: Your team page lists everyone's mobile numbers and the shared login for a supplier portal. Your manager says the page can go online. What do you do first?
options: Publish it, since your manager said yes
Remove the numbers and the login
Publish it and fix anything people flag
steps.why: Published pages are public, so private details must come off before anything goes online. Approval to publish the page isn't approval to publish logins, and fixing it later is too late.
